title: Label Gate, Throat Flora and HACEK Growth
summary: Learn why an unlabeled specimen is rejected rather than relabeled, what normally lives in the throat and what a throat or nasopharyngeal specimen is actually for, and why HACEK organisms grow on blood and chocolate agar in CO2 but not on MacConkey.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 57 Hit 18 (never process or relabel an unlabeled specimen), Hit 37 (oropharyngeal flora; throat versus nasopharyngeal targets) and Exam Trap 5 (HACEK fail to grow on MacConkey). Checked against 42 CFR 493.1242 (eCFR), Lippi 2017, Dikmen 2015, Ning 2016, Baron 2013 (IDSA/ASM guide; the 2018 and 2024 updates were not read), Man 2017, the CDC diphtheria and pertussis laboratory pages, Lee 2018, de Melo Oliveira 2013, Khaledi 2022 and Humphries 2015 (page-fetch tool). Hit 18’s “label immediately after collection, never before” matches CLSI but not WHO or SIBioC (EFLM leaves it to local risk analysis), so the lesson teaches that timing differs. Hit 18’s reject-and-recollect is taught with the irretrievable-specimen exception from one hospital policy. Hit 37 places C. diphtheriae with nasopharyngeal specimens; CDC lists nares, oropharynx and membrane. Trap 5’s “culture-negative endocarditis” is not taught (existing register flag rv-hacek-culture). Not taught: diphtheroids as oropharyngeal residents and “identify by traits, not quantity” (not found in the sources read). Joint Commission and WHO-on-NCBI pages and the NCBI StatPearls MacConkey page were blocked (403/captcha); the Joint Commission goal is taken from Lippi 2017’s summary. The CDC pages returned 403 to direct download and were read via a page-fetch tool.

objectives: Explain why an unlabeled specimen is rejected rather than relabeled, and name the irretrievable-specimen exception.
Name the main residents of the oropharynx and state what throat and nasopharyngeal specimens are used to find.
Describe the growth conditions of HACEK organisms, including failure to grow on MacConkey agar.

scenes.title: Three specimens at the bench
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three specimens reach the microbiology bench. (1) A throat swab with no label; the nurse who sent it offers to come down and write the name on it. (2) A labeled throat swab whose plate shows heavy mixed growth with no beta-hemolytic colonies; the clinician asks for “everything that grows”. (3) A blood culture from a patient with poor dentition and suspected endocarditis: tiny gram-negative rods grow on blood and chocolate agar in CO2, nothing grows on MacConkey. Question token: “Reject, report, or rethink?”

cues.text: Three specimens reach the bench. A throat swab with no label, and a nurse who offers to come and write the name on it.

A labeled throat swab with heavy mixed growth and no beta-hemolytic colonies, and a request to report everything that grows. And a blood culture with tiny gram-negative rods on blood and chocolate agar, but nothing on MacConkey.
For each one: reject, report, or rethink?

scenes.title: Who lives in the throat
scenes.altText: Schematic throat with resident bacteria. Card 1, oropharynx: more diverse than the nasopharynx; streptococcal species, Neisseria species, Rothia and anaerobes such as Veillonella, Prevotella and Leptotrichia (Man 2017). Card 2, nasopharynx: Moraxella, Staphylococcus, Corynebacterium, Dolosigranulum, Haemophilus and Streptococcus. Card 3, HACEK: Haemophilus parainfluenzae, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella and Kingella are fastidious gram-negative bacteria of the normal oral and upper respiratory flora (Khaledi 2022). Token: residents are expected, not reported as infection.

cues.text: The oropharynx is crowded. Its bacterial community is more diverse than the nasopharynx: streptococci, Neisseria species, Rothia, and anaerobes such as Veillonella and Prevotella.
The nasopharynx carries a different set, including Moraxella, staphylococci, corynebacteria, Haemophilus and streptococci.
The HACEK group lives here too: Haemophilus parainfluenzae, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella and Kingella are fastidious gram-negative members of the normal mouth and upper airway flora.
So a throat plate will usually grow residents. The question is whether a target pathogen is there, not whether something grew.

props.label: Growth ≠ infection: look for the target

scenes.title: The label gate
scenes.altText: Gate diagram: specimen → label check → bench. Card 1 (US CLIA, 42 CFR 493.1242): the laboratory must have written policies for specimen labeling (patient name or unique identifier and, when appropriate, source) and for acceptability and rejection. Card 2: at least two patient identifiers, never the room number; containers labeled in the presence of the patient (US Joint Commission goal, as summarized by Lippi 2017). Card 3: unlabeled or mislabeled specimens are rejection criteria (Dikmen 2015); a restrictive acceptance policy (Ning 2016) did not allow relabeling, except for irretrievable specimens such as CSF, tissue or pre-antibiotic blood cultures, where health care staff came to the laboratory in person to identify the specimen and sign the record. Token: tube-labeling timing (before or after filling) differs between guidelines.

cues.text: Before any plate is touched, the specimen passes a label gate. In the United States, CLIA requires written laboratory policies for specimen labeling, with the patient name or a unique identifier, and for specimen acceptance and rejection.
Use at least two patient identifiers, never the room number, and label the container with the patient present. Exactly when to label a blood tube, before or after filling, differs between guidelines.

An unlabeled or mislabeled specimen is a rejection criterion. In one hospital’s restrictive policy, staff could not relabel it at the bench, and specimen identification errors fell after that policy began.

The exception is a specimen that cannot be collected again, such as spinal fluid, tissue, or a blood culture drawn before antibiotics. There, a staff member came to the laboratory in person, identified the specimen, and signed the record.

props.title: Irretrievable exception
lines: Staff ID it in person and sign

scenes.title: Targets and plates
scenes.altText: Three target cards. Throat swab: firm sampling of throat and tonsils, avoiding cheeks, gums and teeth; Streptococcus pyogenes is the most common bacterial cause of pharyngitis; H. influenzae, S. aureus, N. meningitidis and S. pneumoniae are not agents of pharyngitis and are not sought; Arcanobacterium haemolyticum, N. gonorrhoeae and C. diphtheriae are not routinely sought, so the laboratory must be told (Baron 2013). Nasopharyngeal swab or aspirate: Bordetella pertussis by culture and/or NAAT; plate within 24 h (CDC). Diphtheria: swab nares and oropharynx, any lesion, and beneath or part of the membrane (CDC). HACEK card: fastidious gram-negative rods that generally need supplemented media or a CO2-enriched atmosphere and fail to grow on MacConkey (de Melo Oliveira 2013); subculture to sheep blood and chocolate agar at 37 °C in 5–10% CO2 (Khaledi 2022). Hook answers card.

cues.text: A throat culture has one main target: Streptococcus pyogenes, the most common bacterial cause of sore throat. Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus, meningococci and pneumococci do not cause pharyngitis and are not sought.

Rarer throat pathogens, such as Corynebacterium diphtheriae or gonococci, are not looked for routinely, so the clinician must tell the lab. For diphtheria, swab the nose and throat, and beneath the membrane. Pertussis needs a nasopharyngeal swab or aspirate.
HACEK organisms are fastidious gram-negative rods. They grow best on blood and chocolate agar in five to ten percent carbon dioxide, and they fail to grow on MacConkey agar.

Back to the hook. Reject the unlabeled swab and recollect. Report the throat culture for Streptococcus pyogenes, not the residents. And rethink the blood culture: no growth on MacConkey fits a HACEK organism.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “The nurse can label it at the bench” (✓ an unlabeled specimen is rejected; relabeling is reserved for documented irretrievable-specimen exceptions); “Heavy growth on a throat plate means infection” (✓ the oropharynx is full of residents; the throat culture looks for S. pyogenes); “No growth on MacConkey rules out a gram-negative rod” (✓ HACEK are gram-negative rods that fail to grow on MacConkey and want blood/chocolate agar in CO2).

cues.text: Trap one: the nurse can label it at the bench. No: an unlabeled specimen is rejected. Relabeling is kept for documented exceptions with irreplaceable specimens.
Trap two: heavy growth on a throat plate means infection. No: the throat is full of residents. The culture is read for Streptococcus pyogenes.
Trap three: no growth on MacConkey rules out a gram-negative rod. No: HACEK organisms are gram-negative rods that fail on MacConkey and need blood or chocolate agar in carbon dioxide.

props.title: ✗ “Heavy throat growth = infection.”
lines: ✓ Residents expected; look for S. pyogenes

props.title: ✗ “MAC-negative = not a gram-negative rod.”
lines: ✓ HACEK fail on MacConkey; use blood/choc + CO2

cues.text: Memory aid: no name tag, no entry. The throat party has a guest list with one wanted name, Streptococcus pyogenes, among the regular crowd. And the HACEK guests skip the MacConkey bar and wait in the carbon dioxide VIP lounge.

Where it breaks: irreplaceable specimens can have documented exceptions; when to label a tube differs between guidelines; the lab will look for other throat pathogens when asked; and HACEK organisms usually grow in standard blood cultures.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Unlabeled = reject · throat culture = Streptococcus pyogenes among residents”, “HACEK: blood/chocolate + 5–10% CO2 · no growth on MacConkey”.

cues.text: Reject an unlabeled specimen rather than relabel it, read a throat culture for Streptococcus pyogenes among the normal residents, and remember that HACEK organisms are oral gram-negative rods that grow on blood and chocolate agar in carbon dioxide but not on MacConkey.

props.label: Unlabeled = reject · throat culture = S. pyogenes among residents
HACEK: blood/choc + 5–10% CO2 · no growth on MacConkey

explanation.what: Plain language: a specimen without a name cannot be trusted, so the lab sends it back instead of guessing whose it is. The throat is always full of harmless bacteria, so a throat culture hunts for one main troublemaker, group A strep. A small group of mouth bacteria called HACEK are picky gram-negative rods that need rich agar and extra carbon dioxide, and they do not grow on MacConkey. Scientific terms: patient identifiers, specimen rejection criteria, irretrievable specimen, oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal microbiota, Streptococcus pyogenes, Bordetella pertussis, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, fastidious gram-negative rods, capnophilic growth, MacConkey agar.
explanation.why: Identification errors put results on the wrong patient, and in one hospital a strict acceptance policy reduced them. Because throat flora always grows, culturing for everything would report harmless residents as findings. HACEK organisms are part of the oral flora and can cause endocarditis, and their failure to grow on enteric media can hide a gram-negative rod.
explanation.measure: Label: written labeling and rejection policies (US CLIA); at least two identifiers, not the room number; label with the patient present; tube-labeling timing differs by guideline. Unlabeled or mislabeled = rejection criterion; relabeling only as a documented exception for irretrievable specimens (CSF, tissue, pre-antibiotic blood cultures) in one published policy. Throat swab: S. pyogenes; H. influenzae, S. aureus, N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae not sought; C. diphtheriae, N. gonorrhoeae, A. haemolyticum only on request. Diphtheria: nares, oropharynx, membrane. Pertussis: nasopharyngeal swab or aspirate, plate within 24 h. HACEK: blood and chocolate agar at 37 °C, 5–10% CO2; no growth on MacConkey.
explanation.differs: Replaceable vs irretrievable specimens; oropharynx (streptococci, Neisseria, Rothia, anaerobes) vs nasopharynx (Moraxella, staphylococci, corynebacteria, Haemophilus); throat swab (S. pyogenes) vs nasopharyngeal swab (B. pertussis); HACEK (fastidious, MacConkey-negative) vs enteric rods such as Salmonella and Shigella (grow on MacConkey).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the correct action for an unlabeled specimen, which organism a routine throat culture is for, which specimen to collect for pertussis or diphtheria, and which gram-negative rods fail to grow on MacConkey.

takeaway: Reject an unlabeled specimen rather than relabel it, read a throat culture for Streptococcus pyogenes among the normal residents, and remember that HACEK organisms are oral gram-negative rods that grow on blood and chocolate agar in carbon dioxide but not on MacConkey.

questions.stem: A urine container arrives with no label. The nurse who collected it offers to come to the laboratory and write the patient’s name on it. What is the best action?

options.text: Reject the specimen and request a new, correctly labeled collection
options.rationale: Correct. Unlabeled specimens are a rejection criterion, and urine can be collected again.

options.text: Let the nurse label it at the bench and process it
options.rationale: Incorrect. Under a published restrictive acceptance policy, replaceable specimens are not relabeled; urine can be recollected.

options.text: Process it and add a comment that it arrived unlabeled
options.rationale: Incorrect. A comment does not establish whose specimen it is.

options.text: Match it to the only urine order pending in the system
options.rationale: Incorrect. A pending order does not establish whose specimen it is; identity is checked with the patient at collection.

questions.stem: A routine throat culture from a patient with pharyngitis grows heavy mixed flora. Which organism is the routine culture designed to detect?

options.rationale: Correct. It is the most common bacterial cause of pharyngitis and the main target of a throat culture.
Incorrect. It is not an agent of pharyngitis and is not sought in throat cultures.
Incorrect. It is not an agent of pharyngitis and is not sought in throat cultures.

options.text: Neisseria species of the normal flora
options.rationale: Incorrect. Neisseria species are expected residents of the oropharynx.

questions.stem: Blood cultures from a patient with poor dentition grow small gram-negative rods on sheep blood and chocolate agar in 5–10% CO2, with no growth on MacConkey agar. Which group best fits?

options.rationale: Correct. They are fastidious oral gram-negative rods that grow better in CO2 and fail to grow on MacConkey.

options.text: Enteric rods such as Salmonella or Shigella
options.rationale: Incorrect. Salmonella and Shigella grow on MacConkey agar, as colorless lactose-nonfermenting colonies.
Incorrect. Streptococci are gram-positive cocci, not gram-negative rods.

options.text: No organism: MacConkey-negative means the Gram stain was wrong
options.rationale: Incorrect. Failure to grow on MacConkey is expected for fastidious gram-negative rods.

claims.text: Written labeling and rejection policies (US CLIA); at least two identifiers, not the room number; label with the patient present; labeling timing differs by guideline.

Unlabeled or mislabeled specimens are rejection criteria; no relabeling of replaceable specimens; irretrievable-specimen exception with in-person identification and signature; errors fell under the policy.
claims.note: Evidence is one laboratory’s criteria and one hospital’s policy, not a consensus standard.

claims.text: Oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal residents; HACEK as oral and upper respiratory flora.
Throat culture targets S. pyogenes; organisms not sought; rare throat pathogens only on request; diphtheria and pertussis specimen sites; plate pertussis within 24 h.

HACEK: fastidious gram-negative rods, better growth in CO2, blood and chocolate agar at 37 °C in 5–10% CO2, no growth on MacConkey (unlike Salmonella and Shigella); streptococci are gram-positive cocci; usually detected in standard blood cultures.
Reviewer details not taught: diphtheroids as oropharyngeal residents; “identify the pathogen by its traits, not its quantity”; HACEK as culture-negative endocarditis.
claims.note: Diphtheroids were found only among nasal/nasopharyngeal residents in Man 2017; the quantity rule was not found in the sources read; culture-negative status is contradicted by Khaledi 2022 (rv-hacek-culture).

claims.text: Scenario invented; throat and plates schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 57 Hit 18 says to label immediately after collection, never before. Lippi 2017 reports that CLSI labels tubes after filling, WHO and SIBioC before filling, and EFLM WG-PRE leaves it to local risk analysis while always checking identity with the patient present; the lesson teaches that timing differs (register flag rv-ch57-label-timing).

Ch. 57 Hit 18 says reject and recollect without exception. A published restrictive policy (Ning 2016) allows documented relabeling of irretrievable specimens (CSF, tissue, pre-antibiotic blood cultures) when health care personnel identify the specimen in person at the laboratory and sign (register flag rv-ch57-unlabeled-irretrievable).

Ch. 57 Hit 37 assigns C. diphtheriae to nasopharyngeal specimens. CDC lists the nares and oropharynx, lesions and the membrane, and Baron 2013 notes the laboratory must be told to look for it on throat swabs (register flag rv-ch57-diphtheria-specimen).

Ch. 57 Exam Trap 5 links HACEK with culture-negative endocarditis. Khaledi 2022 notes HACEK have been known as blood-culture-negative organisms but reports ~99% detection within the first 5 days by an automated blood-culture system (register flag rv-ch57-trap5-hacek-culture; same issue as rv-hacek-culture for Hit 36).

The labeling and rejection policy requirement taught here is US federal (CLIA), and the two-identifier goal is the US Joint Commission’s. Philippine rules are not covered; MTLE candidates should check local requirements.
